newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan GDP fall doesn't call for economy boost - EPA.
newsitem.headline: Japan GDP fall doesn't call for economy boost - EPA.

text.p: Japan does not have to consider additional government spending aimed at stimulating the economy, despite a decline in gross domestic product (GDP) in the April-June quarter, Economic Planning Agency (EPA) Vice Minister Shinpei Nukaya told a news conference on Friday.
"We don't need to consider additional government spending for the economy following the latest GDP data for April-June," Nukaya said.

Earlier, the EPA announced that GDP fell 0.7 percent in the April-June quarter from the previous quarter, the first quarterly drop since the October-December quarter of 1994, when GDP declined 1.1 percent quarter-on-quarter.

"Speaking from the view of whether we need a supplementary budget to add more government spending for the sake of the economy, we have confirmed that there is steady private-sector capital spending, although consumption still lacks momentum. We are still moving in the direction of a gradual recovery."
Nukaya said the drop in the April-June quarter came as a reaction to extremely strong GDP growth in the previous quarter.
He said that judging from the data for the first two quarters of calendar 1996, "the figures are in line with our view that the economy is recovering gradually."
Excluding the effect of the leap year, GDP would have shown a decline of a scant 0.3 percent quarter-on-quarter in April-June, he said.

Asked if the government wanted to see any change in the Bank of Japan's current monetary stance, Nukaya said: "The Bank of Japan is saying it will maintain its present monetary policy in order to ensure that there is a basis for economic recovery, and we hope the bank will maintain its stance."
Asked if the economic recovery was likely to reach the government's official target of 2.5 percent growth for the current fiscal year ending next March 31, he said it was "highly possible".
He added that in order to reach that goal, GDP would have to show quarter-on-quarter growth of 0.3 percent for the final three quarters of this fiscal year.
He also said the GDP figures for July-September were likely to show an increase due to steady housing investment and a waning of negative effects from weak external demand factors.
"In that sense, we can expect the July-September figure to show a moderate recovery."

Asked whether the government should continue special income tax cuts into the next fiscal year, Nukaya said it would depend on the economic outlook for that year, which would become clear towards the end of December.
He also said a reported decrease in planned capital spending by the semiconductor industry would not have a major impact on private-sector capital investment plans as a whole.
